items.title: Georgian England had 200+ capital offences

options.text: A modernised criminal code that abolished hanging
The expansion of capital crimes from around 50 in 1688 to over 220 by 1815 — including stealing goods worth 12 pence from a shop
A medieval system of trial by ordeal
The system of cattle thieves' execution in Scotland only

items.reveal:
The Waltham Black Act (1723) alone created around 50 new capital offences. Many capital sentences were commuted (juries undervalued goods to avoid death penalty — 'pious perjury'), or replaced by transportation to America (until 1776) and Australia (from 1787).

Reformers — Samuel Romilly, Robert Peel as Home Secretary — gradually reduced the list. By 1841 only treason, murder and a handful of others remained capital. Public hangings at Tyburn ended in 1783 (moved to Newgate); the last public hanging was 1868.
items.why: The Bloody Code shows the early modern state using execution as a substitute for an effective police force. The Victorian shift to imprisonment + policing changes the whole structure of criminal justice.

items.title: The Plague of Athens (430 BCE) killed perhaps a quarter of the population
items.claim: What was the Plague of Athens?

options.text: An epidemic (possibly typhus, smallpox or typhoid — debated) hit Athens 430-426 BCE during the Peloponnesian War, killing perhaps 75,000-100,000 including Pericles; described in detail by Thucydides who survived the disease himself
The same outbreak as the 1665 London plague

items.reveal:
Thucydides' 'History of the Peloponnesian War' (Book II) records the symptoms in clinical detail — fever, redness of the eyes, internal ulceration, severe thirst. He notes that survivors gained immunity. The cause remains debated; DNA evidence from Athenian mass graves (2006) tentatively suggested typhoid fever.

Pericles, the city's leading statesman, died of the plague in autumn 429 BCE. The disease wrecked Athenian morale and military capacity early in the war with Sparta, which Athens eventually lost in 404 BCE.

Thucydides is sometimes called 'the father of scientific history' — his account of the plague aimed to provide future generations with a description that would help them recognise it.
items.why: Ancient epidemics had political consequences. The death of Pericles changed the leadership of Athens at a critical moment; the disease's social effects — Thucydides describes breakdown of religious and legal norms — anticipate modern observations on epidemic societies.

items.title: The Great Pyramid was the world's tallest building for 3,800 years
items.claim: How tall is the Great Pyramid and how long did it hold the height record?

options.text: Originally around 146.7 m (now around 138.5 m after loss of casing stones), built around 2560 BCE for Pharaoh Khufu — the tallest human structure until Lincoln Cathedral's spire (around 160 m) in 1311 CE
It has been the world's tallest building continuously

items.reveal:
The Great Pyramid of Giza was built during the Fourth Dynasty for Khufu (Greek: Cheops). It contains around 2.3 million blocks averaging 2.5 tonnes each. The construction took perhaps 20 years using rotating labour gangs (around 20,000-30,000 workers at peak).

Lincoln Cathedral's central spire (completed around 1311) finally exceeded it. That spire collapsed in 1549. The Eiffel Tower (1889) finally and permanently dethroned the pyramid as the world's tallest human structure.

The original outer casing of polished white Tura limestone was largely removed in medieval Cairo for building material — including for the Hassan Mosque (1356).
items.why: Scale matters in human achievement. A building completed 4,500 years ago held the height record for 3,800 of those years — a testament to ancient engineering that modern construction took until the 19th century to surpass.
